prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and should teach it with more confidence than many of them currently do, because a fluent running hand is a cheap and durable tool that carries children through fifteen years of note-taking, drafting and examinations, while the case for dropping it depends on a picture of adult life in which nobody writes anything by hand, a picture that does not match what happens in classrooms, exam halls or most people's working days.

The argument against deserves to be put at full strength, since it is made by thoughtful people: children meet tablets before they meet pencils, adults handwrite little beyond shopping lists and birthday cards, the keyboard is the instrument most of them will earn a living with, and every hour spent on entry strokes and consistent letter height is an hour taken from composition, from reading, or from touch-typing, which has an obvious payoff. Finland made the best-known move in this direction when it removed compulsory cursive from its national core curriculum in the middle of the last decade and left schools to decide how much handwriting of any kind to teach, a decision its defenders present as plain realism about the tools children will use. If the only question were which skill has the more visible commercial value in 2040, the keyboard would win without much of a contest. The question is a different one, because schools are not only preparing children for jobs but building the cognitive habits that make reading, spelling and composition possible, and on that ground handwriting has a stronger record than its critics allow.

When a child writes a letter by hand, the letter has to be constructed from a sequence of movements, whereas on a keyboard it is selected from a row of identical keys, and the research on young children suggests that this difference matters. Studies by Karin James and colleagues found that preschoolers who practised letters by hand showed more activity in the brain regions associated with reading than children who typed or traced the same letters, and the long programme of work by Virginia Berninger and by Steve Graham and his co-authors has repeatedly found that explicit handwriting instruction improves not just legibility but the quantity and quality of what children write. The mechanism is easy to understand once it is stated: a child who has to think about how to form each letter is spending working memory on the pen, and so has less left for the sentence, the spelling and the idea, while a child whose letters come automatically can give attention to what is being said. Fluent handwriting is therefore a precondition for fluent composition in the early years, which is why a school that neglects it will see the cost later in thin, hesitant and short pieces of writing from children who clearly have more to say than they can get down.

It would be dishonest to claim that this evidence settles the narrower question of joined versus printed script, because most of it compares handwriting with typing or compares taught with untaught handwriting, and the studies that compare cursive with print directly are mixed, with some finding no difference in speed or legibility once children have practised enough. A well-taught printed hand can be quick and clear, and the claims sometimes made for cursive, that it improves intelligence or unlocks some special cognitive pathway, are not supported. Even the celebrated finding that students remember lecture material better when they take notes longhand than when they type has been only partly replicated, with later studies reporting smaller effects. The argument for joined-up writing therefore cannot rest on magic. It rests on a more modest judgement, which is that handwriting is going to remain part of school life for the foreseeable future, so the sensible question is which script gives children the best return on the limited time they spend learning it, and on that question joined writing has real advantages.

The first is mechanical, since printing lifts the pen at every letter and joined writing does not, so that a word becomes a single continuous gesture in place of a string of separate stops. A single gesture is faster once it is learned, and it also turns spelling patterns into motor sequences, so that the endings of words like walking, nation and through are practised by the hand as units and are remembered partly in the fingers, which is a real help to children who find spelling difficult. A second advantage is that a script built on entry strokes makes the shapes that children most often confuse start in different places, which is why teachers in many countries report fewer reversals of b and d when children learn joined forms from the beginning, and a third is that words written in a continuous line look like words, with clear gaps between them, where printed letters tend to float apart and drift off the line. The fourth is that teaching one system from the start avoids the waste involved in teaching print in reception and then asking seven-year-olds to unlearn half of it, which is what happens in the schools that treat joining as an optional extra to be added when time allows. Most adults who write by hand at volume end up with some kind of semi-joined hand anyway, because pure print is slow over a three-hour examination, and a school that teaches the join properly gives children sound letter shapes to build that personal hand on, where one that does not leaves them to improvise it badly at fourteen under time pressure.

Examinations are the plainest place to see why this matters. In England, in much of the United States, and in most of the world, the great majority of high-stakes assessment is still written by hand on paper, and a student sitting a run of three-hour papers in the summer needs to produce thousands of words legibly and at speed, with examiners on record complaining each year about scripts they cannot read. A child with a slow, effortful hand is disadvantaged in every one of those papers, whatever they know, and the disadvantage falls hardest on children whose homes offer no extra practice. There is an equity argument here that tends to be overlooked in discussions that assume every child has a laptop: a pencil and paper are the one writing technology that every child in the class can afford, which needs no charging, no connection and no licence, and which does not offer a notification, a game or a search bar when attention wavers. Then there is reading, because the script that adults write in is not confined to the examination hall, and a child who cannot read cursive cannot read the comments a teacher writes in the margin, the letters their grandparents send, or the archive documents that historians and genealogists work from, which is why the American debate over cursive has been partly a debate about whether a generation should be able to read the Constitution in the hand it was written in. Several American states that dropped cursive after the adoption of the common standards have since legislated to bring it back, and the reasons they give have more to do with literacy than with nostalgia.

The practical objections are worth meeting directly. The first is that handwriting crowds out more valuable teaching, and the answer is that it takes far less time than is often assumed when it is taught systematically, with perhaps ten minutes a day in the early years, whereas the lessons that do consume time are the unsystematic ones in which children are told to take more care and left to work out how. The case here is for better teaching of handwriting, delivered briefly and consistently, and not for more hours of it. The second objection concerns the minority of children with dysgraphia or other motor difficulties, for whom joined writing can be a misery, and there the response is to provide keyboards, occupational therapy and extra time without delay and without stigma, while recognising that a curriculum designed around its hardest case fails the large majority who would have learned the skill without difficulty. Some specialists who work with dyslexic children actually prefer continuous script for the reasons given above, though the research on this is thin and nobody should pretend otherwise. The third objection is aesthetic, that children are marked down for untidy hands, and that is a fair complaint about a bad way of teaching, since the goals should be legibility and fluency and not elegance, and no child should lose marks for having an individual style that others can read perfectly well.

None of this requires a choice between pens and keyboards, and the schools that do best are likely to be those that teach both, with joined handwriting established by about seven and touch-typing introduced soon afterwards, so that by eleven a child can move comfortably between the two and choose the right one for the task. What a school should not do is treat handwriting as a relic that will fade away of its own accord, because the evidence says that the skill supports reading, spelling and composition, the assessment system still demands it, and the children with the least at home depend on the school to teach it. Joined-up writing is the most efficient way to teach it that we have, and a school that drops it in the name of the future is likely to find that the future, for its pupils, still includes a three-hour paper and a pen.
